claims.text: A learning-based approach calibrated with multiscale atomistic descriptors will accurately identify new HEAs with anomalously low phonon thermal conductivity.
Multi-principal-element high-entropy materials can exhibit substantial local strain and chemical-bonding variation.
Local strain, bonding fluctuations, and electronegativity differences are suitable descriptors for modeling lattice thermal conductivity.
The proposed descriptors can be used to calibrate a learning-based model from a training set of previously characterized HEAs.
The approach is applicable to alloys compositionally similar to its training data, exemplified by alloys containing five to seven principal elements and strong local chemical fluctuations.
Differences in atomic mass contribute to local elemental or chemical fluctuations.
Electronegativity differences create variations in local chemical bonding.
Strong elemental fluctuations induce lattice distortion and strain fluctuations.
Lattice distortion and strain fluctuations strengthen phonon scattering.
Enhanced phonon scattering caused by local fluctuations reduces lattice thermal conductivity.
Modeling local lattice distortions will distinguish low-conductivity HEAs better than conventional models based solely on average compositional properties.
The approach will identify candidates whose lattice thermal conductivity is at least 20% lower than values predicted by traditional methods.
Current predictive models rely on conventional compositional or averaged thermodynamic parameters without detailed multiscale atomistic calibration.
The approach may not generalize to compositions outside the training regime.
Unmodeled phase separation or non-stoichiometric effects may limit predictions of phonon scattering.
The proposed 20% improvement estimate is based on limited training data and may vary among alloy systems.
Atomic-resolution chemical mapping can characterize local elemental fluctuations.

Failure to observe a statistically significant reduction of at least 20% relative to the control group, or failure of measured local fluctuations to correlate with predictions, would falsify the hypothesis.
